Why must we state that it is not solitary? The proponent of the philosophical tenet <note>refers to the logical-epistemological school of Dignaga and Dharmakirti</note> says: because it is momentary. The specific nature of this thing, which is simultaneous with its cooperating causes, has been its own first momentary nature since beginningless cyclic existence <term>samsara</term> <gloss>the cycle of death and rebirth</gloss>. Therefore, its nature is certain to be momentary. How could it be solitary?

If one thinks: it must also be proven that a functional thing <term>bhavas</term> <gloss>entities</gloss> existing for only a single moment produces an effect, for that reason the text says: how it produces has already been explained. Just as it produces an effect while remaining for a single moment, it was already explained above in the section: they do not exist before and do not exist after, nor do they have a separate nature.

When that is the case, how could that thing which possesses power and produces an effect without interruption — having the quality of arising in a single moment — exist before, after, or separately? Because it has a nature that arises from only a single moment, it is characterized as arising in a single moment. In some volumes, the phrase arising in that moment appears. This should be understood as follows: because it has a nature that arises only in that specific intended moment, the phrase arising in that moment is applied. 

Before, after, and separate are explained here as terms for change. If one thinks: we clearly see change in things like seeds which, when not yet gathered into a collection, exist before, and then exist separately after being removed from the collection; for that reason the text says: that which changes, and so forth. That which is not gathered into a collection, or that which is separated from a collection to act individually, is not the same entity that possesses the quality of producing an effect without delay. Therefore, the consequence was stated: why does a momentary thing not produce effects solitarily, and why is it not solitary?

<summary>This page discusses the Buddhist logical argument that functional entities are momentary and must rely on a collection of causes rather than acting in isolation. It refutes the idea of a permanent or solitary cause by asserting that the nature of an entity is inseparable from its immediate capacity to produce an effect.</summary>
<keywords>momentariness, causation, cooperating causes, functional entities, Buddhist logic, samsara, change</keywords>

Regarding that, being authentic means that non-deception is not undermined. Why is this? Because in a dream, it occurs again either in that same way or in another. The phrase "this is" refers to experiencing great joy. The phrase "because it is known" means that precisely at that time, because it is experienced as functioning, it is non-deceptive. Therefore, the meaning is that waking and dreaming are established as valid cognition <term>pramana</term> <gloss>reliable means of knowledge</gloss> and its opposite, respectively, through being non-deceptive and the alternative.

If one thinks: "Since we see the nature of dreaming and its opposite, and they are already distinguished as being false and the alternative, what other cause for distinction is needed?" To this, he says "dreaming and the other." Mere individual appearance does not create the distinction between that and the other, because there is no difference between them. The meaning is that the distinction between deception and the alternative is not established.

Does it not seem unreasonable for the Mimamsaka <note>original: "skyes mos", referring to the Mimamsa school of Indian philosophy</note> to say, "Because there is no object of observation <term>alambana</term> <gloss>the objective support of consciousness</gloss> for this"? Because saying "it does not exist" is not the object of observation; rather, the statement "it does not exist" is itself the observation.

Thinking that if one is separated from the secondary dependence, no knowledge would arise at all, he says "the cognition that this does not exist." The phrase "realized by another" refers to realization through direct perception <term>pratyaksha</term> or inference <term>anumana</term>. Forms, tastes, and so on are realized by the direct perception in which they appear. Therefore, existence itself is not apparent because it is void of and separated from the other. Because it is of a nature void of that, it is known; even if it is not known by the appropriate subjects, it is known by itself. The cognition that follows direct perception of only the nature separated from that is intended to be the producer of its own form. Therefore, to show that the object of observation here is nothing other than what is intended, he says "it has become like that." This also arises from habitual tendencies <term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious imprints</gloss> which are specified.

<summary>This page discusses the epistemological distinction between waking reality and dreams, focusing on the criteria for non-deceptive knowledge and the role of mental imprints in perception.</summary>
<keywords>non-deception, dream, valid cognition, pramana, object of observation, alambana, Mimamsa, habitual tendencies, vasana</keywords>

Even that which lacks an essence would be subject to birth and death, much like a person who is the object of desire. However, this is not the case because there is no distinction <note>between the two scenarios in such an illogical framework</note>. If that were so, then even confusion without a seed — which appears as an inversion of reality — would not occur.

That is not the nature of reality itself. By whom <note>is this perceived</note>? By all those who do not see the supreme. This refers to everyone other than the Buddha, those whose state is corrupted by the subject-object duality <term>grahya-grahaka</term> <gloss>the apprehended and the apprehender</gloss>. Only the Buddha knows reality as it truly is; others do not.

Even though the Blessed Buddha has analyzed the very nature of this inversion, he establishes it in accordance with how it is seen <note>by ordinary beings</note>. In this way, the cause of their attachment is shown. Since those who do not see the supreme cannot perceive reality, the text mentions "apprehended" and so forth; this is because for those who do not see the supreme, there is no state that is not corrupted by the apprehended and the apprehender.

Because they are always corrupted by the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender, such a corrupted vision is not supreme or transcendent. Since they lack the vision of the supreme, which is devoid of these two <note>subject and object</note>, how could they know reality? This is because the latencies <term>vasana</term> <gloss>habitual tendencies</gloss> of the two have not been uprooted. When they see what is devoid of these two, then they will see reality, because reality is characterized by being devoid of these two.

Therefore, for that reason, the Blessed Buddhas — who treat the meaning of reality with equanimity <note>original: "upeksha"</note> and whose nature is free from the characteristics of the objects of reality — perform the "gaze of the elephant." Just as an elephant looks back, although they have seen the reality of things, they act as if they do not see it themselves. Solely out of concern for the world, they engage in external conduct. They act for the sake of the appearances to which the world is attached. They teach: Understand things exactly as they appear; do not grasp at what contradicts how things appear. Thus, they establish the characteristics of internal and external things.

<summary>This page discusses the nature of reality as being free from the subject-object duality and explains why only a Buddha can perceive it truly. It describes how Buddhas use skillful means, such as the elephant's gaze, to engage with the world's conventional perceptions while remaining in a state of equanimity.</summary>
<keywords>subject-object duality, Buddha-knowledge, inversion of reality, elephant's gaze, equanimity, latencies, appearances</keywords>

<meta>The text is a philosophical commentary from the Derge Tengyur, specifically the Logic volume (Tshad ma), dealing with formal syllogisms and the relationship between the subject, the predicate, and the logical reason.</meta>

It is the <term>subject</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: dharmin; the thing being discussed</gloss>. Therefore, when it is said that it is pervaded by one portion of the direction of the property of the <term>subject</term> <gloss>dharmin</gloss> that is to be proven, the pervasion by the property of the <term>probandum</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: sādhya; the thing to be proven</gloss> will be understood. If one asks: "Is the subject itself not a portion of that?" indeed that is true, but pervasion by that is impossible, because it is of the nature of a specific distinction. 

If one objects: "It is not that pervasion is absent in the distinction, it is just not understood," that is not the case. Pervasion is of the nature of positive and negative concomitance <note>original: "rjes su 'gro ldog"; Sanskrit: anvaya-vyatireka; the presence of the reason where the predicate is present, and its absence where the predicate is absent</note>. Furthermore, since these are of a nature that exists in all things, such a distinction is impossible. Therefore, the meaning of the statement "the pervasion of the property of the <term>subject</term> <gloss>dharmin</gloss> by the property of the <term>probandum</term> <gloss>sādhya</gloss> is the <term>logical reason</term> <gloss>Sanskrit: hetu</gloss>" will be understood.

Having explained the phrase "by a part of that property of the position," the term "pervasion" <gloss>Sanskrit: vyāpti</gloss> is mentioned in order to explain it. Pervasion is called such because the <term>pervaded</term> <gloss>vyāpya</gloss> is covered by the <term>pervader</term> <gloss>vyāpaka</gloss>. To express this is to express the specific nature determined by them individually. Therefore, the specific nature of the pervader is expressed exactly as it is; there is no separate "action" at all.

In this context, there are three types of restriction to be grasped within the three words: 
1. Restriction to that itself.
2. Restriction only to the qualifier.
3. Restriction to existence itself.

In order to understand the pervader, it is appropriate to understand the qualified itself. Thus, it is taught that "the pervasion by that part is the <term>logical reason</term> <gloss>hetu</gloss>." It is taught that because the presence and absence of the <term>pervaded</term> <gloss>vyāpya</gloss> exist in the qualifier itself, and because those very things establish the reason as the means of comprehension. 

Therefore, when the nature of the means of comprehension is expressed by saying "if the proof exists, the thing to be proven is individually determined to exist," it must be stated as "the pervader definitely exists." If one were to restrict it as "only the pervader exists," the property that acts as the means of comprehension would not be shown, because the <term>pervaded</term> <gloss>vyāpya</gloss> is present...

<summary>This page discusses the logical mechanics of pervasion (vyāpti) and how the relationship between the logical reason and the property to be proven must be restricted to ensure valid cognition. It analyzes the specific nature of qualifiers and the necessity of positive and negative concomitance in a syllogism.</summary>
<keywords>pervasion, vyāpti, logical reason, hetu, subject, dharmin, probandum, sādhya, concomitance, anvaya-vyatireka, Buddhist logic</keywords>

<meta>The text is a philosophical commentary from the Tengyur, specifically focusing on Pramana (Logic and Epistemology). It discusses the concept of Exclusion (Apoha) in relation to linguistic meaning and cognition.</meta>

One should not accept <term>Apoha</term> <gloss>exclusion of others</gloss> as the primary object of sound, because this would be a denial <note>original: "de 'gegs pa'i phyir ro"</note>. To address this, it is stated: "That is not a deceiver." 

The phrase "That is" refers to things other than <term>Apoha</term>, such as the sounds themselves. The phrase "it is a deceiver" means that it does not function without deception <note>it is not non-deceptive</note>. Alternatively, because there is no non-deceptive quality in this, it is called a deceiver.

Why is this so? It is because the connection with the actual <term>vastu</term> <gloss>functional entity/thing</gloss> has been lost. Because there is no connection with such an entity, and because it was previously refuted that the meaning of a sound is a real entity characterized by a universal <term>samanya</term> <gloss>generality/class</gloss> and so forth.

If that is the case, how does the cognition arise which refutes the meaning of sound as <term>Apoha</term> <gloss>exclusion</gloss> from sounds other than that? In response, it says: "All cognitions arising from sound..."

Some cognitions arising from sound are produced simply through the power of the habitual tendencies <term>vasana</term> <gloss>subconscious imprints</gloss> of cultivated conceptual thought that does not correspond to reality. Because of the mere arising of such an attachment to unreal objects, things do not become existent or non-existent based on that power.

Regarding the statement starting with "The sound of the 'knowable' <term>jñeya</term>...", it mentions the sound of the "knowable" and so forth. Concerning what is being expressed, it is asked: "To what does it refer when saying there is nothing to be excluded by the sound of 'knowable' and so forth?"

First, if one relies on the sound of "knowable" and the like as a mere isolated word not residing in a sentence and lacking connection with other words, then it would be a case of proving what is already established <note>a logical fallacy where the conclusion is already accepted</note>. This is because it is pointless and there is no application of an isolated term.

To demonstrate this, it says: "By those possessing discernment, suddenly..." 

Here, "isolated" means disconnected from other words. "Suddenly" means outside of the specific context. The reason why those with discernment apply sounds <note>use language</note> is for the sake of helping the listener, not out of mere attachment. By using an isolated term, a listener cannot be helped through the reversal of doubt and error.

In this way, if a teacher reverses the doubt and erroneous mind that has arisen in a listener regarding an isolated term, and thereby produces a knowledge free of doubt, then they have helped that person; otherwise, <unclear>sentence continues to next page</unclear>

<summary>This page discusses the epistemological status of Apoha (exclusion) and why isolated words fail to communicate effectively or connect with reality without context. It argues that linguistic meaning is often driven by habitual mental tendencies rather than direct contact with functional entities.</summary>
<keywords>Apoha, exclusion, cognition, semantics, Pramana, habitual tendencies, listener, doubt, conceptual thought</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical analysis of logical reasons within the Epistemology (Pramana) section of the Tengyur. It specifically addresses the critique of the "three characteristics" of a logical reason, arguing that the essential quality is "inseparability" or "impossibility without the other."</meta>

Nor is there a fourth <note>category or characteristic</note>. For example, even if there are three sons, because one son is particularly cherished, the world says: "He has an only son." In the same way, one should view the matter here. Because of the connection of "not occurring if [the other] is absent," <note>the principle of essential connection or 'avinabhava'</note> it is never the case that the three modes <note>the 'trirupa' or three characteristics of a valid reason: presence in the subject, presence in the similar class, and absence in the dissimilar class</note> exist independently. In that portion which is otherwise impossible, one observes the existence of the reason <note>the 'hetu' or logical evidence</note>.

Whatever is "impossible otherwise" is itself the logical reason. Whether the two examples <note>the similar and dissimilar examples used in formal logic</note> exist or not, they are not the actual cause of the realization. Where "impossibility otherwise" exists, what use is there for the three modes?

He is dark-complexioned because he is that father's son, just like the appearance of the other <note>siblings</note>. In this case, although it possesses the three modes, it does not function because of certainty. Aside from those two examples, it is a logical reason of a single characteristic. Whether a thing is an entity or a non-entity, it is perceived as having its own identity in whatever way it may be.

Because it is called "the Moon," the "Marked by a Hare" <note>a common epithet for the moon in Indo-Tibetan culture</note> is not "not the moon." This is the second characteristic.

Other logical reasons should also be mentioned. From the touch of a gadfly landing, a perception arises; one knows for certain: "This sensation was caused by the presence of a gadfly." Regarding the activity of perceiving form, the eye is fully possessed of the capacity; this is because it performs that activity and because it sees.

Furthermore, the self, a pot, and so on, are in every way non-existent in nature because they are not perceived in any way, just like horns connected to a donkey. Also, a hare's horn and such are in every way existent in nature because they are perceived in whatever way, for example, like the self and a son.

"Your father is in this house" is something to be known, because the very voice of your father is heard in this house. In the case of entities like sound and a butter lamp, there is the quality of "impossibility otherwise." Even if the "property of the subject" <note>the 'paksadharmata' or first mode of the reason</note> is absent as a thing, it is seen to function as a means of realization.

Therefore, a logical reason with a single characteristic is the primary means of realization. What use do you have for the examination of other useless things like the "property of the subject"? Does one realize that logical reason endowed with this characteristic through a generality, or is it desired to be known—

<summary>This page critiques the traditional three-mode requirement for logical reasons, arguing that the single principle of "inseparability" or "impossibility otherwise" is sufficient for valid inference. It provides various examples including family traits, sensory perceptions, and household sounds to illustrate how certainty is established.</summary>
<keywords>logic, inference, three modes, inseparability, epistemology, pramāṇa, logical reason, perception</keywords>

It has already been shown that the existence of a thing is its very nature. If that is so, how can fire that does not produce smoke still be considered fire? Or how can smoke produced by smoke still be considered smoke? This fault does not apply here, because we have accepted a distinction between types of fire and smoke, rather than referring to fire in a general sense. While we deny that anything other than fire can be the cause, we do not claim that all fire must be the cause <note>of smoke</note>. Alternatively, this is not the case because fire is never divorced from its capacity to produce smoke; it has been explained elsewhere that from the moment of its arising, fire does not deviate from its nature of providing assistance <note>acting as a causal agent</note>.

If there exists fire that does not produce smoke, then is it not the case that fire in general is not the producer of smoke? Therefore, just as with characteristics such as momentariness, this is a specific distinction. If this is so, then even if the specific distinction is separated from the fire itself, it would become something else. Or, if it is said that smoke must be described as unerringly tied to the cause, fire, in another way: It is said that even if fire possesses specific distinctions, it certainly possesses distinctions that constitute its own essence. If this were not so, then because the specific distinctions would be different while the fire itself remained identical, one would be forced to accept a universal <term>samanya</term> <gloss>a general category or abstract essence</gloss>.

Therefore, just as things are distinct by the nature of fire itself, they are also distinct by being producers of smoke and non-producers of smoke; thus, there is no fault at all. When the head of <term>Indra</term> <gloss>the king of the gods, here used in a logical syllogism</gloss> is of a nature that is not fire, if smoke were to arise from that non-fire head of Indra, then that <note>the head</note> would become the cause, fire. If smoke does not arise from what is not fire—because it does not arise from what is dissimilar, because different causes produce different effects, and because the production of smoke is the very form of fire—then one describes smoke as being unerringly related to fire. 

How then can smoke arise from dissimilar, distinct auxiliary causes and from what is not fire? This is addressed by the statement: Now, then, regarding those <note>results</note> arising from distinct auxiliary causes. Those <note>causes</note> are dissimilar by their very distinctness and possess a nature that is not fire. By the method already explained, the fruit...

<summary>This page discusses the causal relationship between fire and smoke, arguing that specific causal capacities are inherent to the essence of an object rather than being external attributes. It defends the necessity of a specific cause for a specific effect to avoid the logical fallacy of universal categories.</summary>
<keywords>causality, fire and smoke, logic, Buddhist philosophy, nature of existence, Indra, universal, specific distinction</keywords>

<meta>The text continues the analysis of Buddhist logic and epistemology, specifically addressing the nature of destruction, persistence, and the relationship between consciousness and its objects.</meta>

It is stated as a direct example of cognition. For this reason <note>original: དེའི་ཕྱིར་ "de'i phyir"</note> refers to the conclusion of the refutation of a supporting basis. What is the point of speaking at length? For a moment, consider whether a thing that perishes depends on another or does not depend on another. In the first case, there is no purpose for a cause that maintains that thing's existence, because if the destroyer is not present, the thing persists by itself. In the second case, there is likewise no capacity <note>for a cause to prevent destruction</note>. The word "all" <note>original: རྣམས་ "rnams"</note> is a plural term used to express clarity. If a support makes the state of destruction occur through itself or another, then at that time, everything that has the nature of arising would possess a supporting state of existence. The rest is easy to understand.

Furthermore, consider whether the object to be maintained is itself perishing or not perishing. Here too, respectively, there is either an inability or a lack of necessity. Previously, the distinction was made by investigating the very position of destruction accepted by others, thereby establishing the two faults. Regarding the summary, it is intended to be expressed as having a remainder. This means these are verses that summarize what was explicitly stated and what was implied.

In the ultimate sense <term>paramārtha</term> <gloss>absolute truth</gloss>, that which abides in an object does not actually meet with the object. Why is that? It is because of the "mind." The "its" refers to the object's. The intention is that the mental consciousness itself, which performs the connection, is the "being" <term>sattva</term>. If it is argued that even in non-conceptual <note>original: རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་མེད་པ་ "rtog pa med pa"</note> cognition there is nothing other than the mere aspect of meeting the object, that is true. In non-conceptual cognition, the convention of "meeting" is compatible because there is a clear experience of the aspect of that object. However, for conceptual thought, this is not the case, because it follows the divisions of the object and the aspect. For that very reason, it is said "in the ultimate sense."

A lamp has a nature characterized by both waning and increasing. Because those things are of such a nature, the fuel <term>upādāna</term> <gloss>appropriation/material cause</gloss> and that which arises from the fuel—the light and the lamp—exist in a relationship of support and supported. How that occurs, and how this very transformation as the characteristic of the fuel is faultless, has already been explained previously. Again, repeating...

<summary>This page analyzes the logical contradictions in the concept of a "supporting cause" for persistent things and discusses the relationship between mental consciousness and perceived objects in both conceptual and non-conceptual states.</summary>
<keywords>destruction, support, mental consciousness, conceptual thought, non-conceptual, ultimate sense, lamp analogy, cause and effect</keywords>

It is clearly shown, meaning it is explained clearly. To explain is to describe the specific nature of the transformation and so forth. Regarding the phrase from what cause: this refers to the cause of cognition, and it is connected to the object of observation. No matter which word it depends on, the meaning is extracted from that cause. At that very time, it should be connected by saying that causes such as hatred are closely observed.

Alternatively, the phrase from what cause relates to the preceding section. Depending on which cause, such as the <term>rlung</term> <gloss>wind/humor</gloss>, results in the cause of desire and so forth, it should be applied to the phrase whatever specific transformation. The phrase at that time should be placed before the words because of that cause, depending on which word it relates to, and then applied to the phrase the nature of all things.

Because desire and other emotions are not certain to arise from bile and the other humors, they do not constitute the nature of everything. Furthermore, the specific states dwelling in bile and the other humors would become the nature of every specific instance of desire and so forth. This is because the error would be the same. It is because of that cause which makes desire and so forth appear as identical.

If one wonders how this could be incorrect, the text says and that too, referring to the specific transformation of <term>bad kan</term> <gloss>phlegm/humor</gloss> and so forth. Even if any particular condition of the wind humor or others were the cause, not every specific instance would possess all forms of desire and so forth. One must infer this because a certain result is seen at all times.

To anticipate an objection, the text says but if the result, because it is accompanied by a certain specific cooperative cause. In that case, that specific cooperative cause of a certain result is nothing other than habituation. This is because the distinctions in desire and so forth are seen to arise from the distinctions in habituation. If one imagines another cause, then even smoke would not be established as having fire as its cause. The response to this is the phrase just as smoke where no fire is seen. Because smoke is possessed of fire, fire exists in that place. Therefore, fire itself is the cause of smoke, not the location. If one thinks this, the text says it is not so, raising a doubt <unclear>one or two words at page break</unclear>

<summary>This page discusses the causal relationship between physical humors and mental afflictions like desire and hatred. It argues that mental states are primarily driven by habituation rather than purely physical causes, using the classic analogy of smoke and fire to illustrate logical necessity.</summary>
<keywords>causality, humors, wind, phlegm, bile, desire, habituation, logic, smoke and fire analogy</keywords>

<meta>The text continues from a discussion regarding the nature of objects and conceptual cognition within the context of Buddhist logic and epistemology.</meta>

The nature of that <note>the object of cognition</note> cannot be definitively established as its own objective domain. Because that conceptualization arises from the habitual tendencies <note>original: <term>vasana</term> <gloss>karmic imprints or latencies</gloss></note> produced by the cognition of existence, non-existence, or both, it is described as the property of things, non-things, or both, due to the power of adhering to the appearances that manifest within it. 

Therefore, regarding the entities dwelling in that subject, one ponders whether this appearing object, derived from the sound of the "Primal Nature" <note>original: <term>Prakriti</term> <gloss>the fundamental matter in Samkhya philosophy</gloss></note>, is something that possesses a substantial cause in reality, or if it is not, thereby considering it in terms of existence and non-existence. 

In establishing that it does not possess a substantial cause in reality, that object which is not to be rejected because it is individually self-cognized <note>original: <term>svasamvedana</term> <gloss>self-awareness or reflexive awareness</gloss></note> is the subject. It cannot be said that this object is a specifically characterized thing <note>original: <term>svalaksana</term> <gloss>a real, unique particular</gloss></note>. This is because it does not disappear even in relation to objects that have not been obtained or have ceased to exist, and because it also appears to the cognitions of other non-Buddhist philosophers who possess inverted attachments toward functional things. 

If words were to engage solely with ultimate reality <note>original: <term>paramartha</term></note>, then the words of those with different philosophical views would not engage with objects without a cause. Furthermore, regarding the past and the unborn <note>future</note>, no words at all would have a false <unclear>false</unclear> object. For this reason, these are asserted to have the objects of the mind as their domain. 

These are the summary verses: 

In the process of proving that it does not possess a substantial cause of the nature one desires, the proof is not unestablished because there exists the property of non-perception. Here, the object appearing to the conceptualization of the sound is not denied either. This is because the sound is applied to the object as it is placed in the mind, and because without that <note>mental image</note>, the sound would be improper.

Furthermore:
Those who do not deny the meaning of words
Must analyze the functional thing itself
Through the distinctions of the sides of existence and non-existence,
Because the arising of the result depends upon it.

Whether the object of the sound exists or does not exist, the purpose of a person is neither slightly damaged nor accomplished. This is because it is not the suchness <note>original: <term>tathata</term> <gloss>ultimate reality</gloss></note> as it is adhered to, and because...

<summary>This page discusses the relationship between conceptual thought, language, and reality, arguing that words refer to mental constructs rather than ultimate, specifically characterized things. It critiques the idea that language directly corresponds to external existence, emphasizing that verbal objects are products of habitual mental tendencies.</summary>

<keywords>conceptualization, habitual tendencies, Primal Nature, self-cognition, specifically characterized thing, ultimate reality, non-perception, mental object</keywords>

Regarding the statement **whatever the nature of cessation is** and so forth: there are two types of destruction: the nature of the interruption of a continuum, and the characteristic of arising as a dissimilar continuum. Regarding these, if one speaks in terms of destruction as the nature of the interruption of a continuum, that is incorrect. Concerning the phrase **it does not exist even at the end**, since it lacks an essence, why would one say **how could it exist even at the end**? Therefore, because this is never accepted as existing at any time, the consequence that the thing does not exist at the beginning or the end is simply irrelevant.

Similarly, it is only a refutation of the arising that occurs through the connection of subsequent moments of the same type. The meaning is that when a pot and such things are said to be destroyed, that very thing does not arise again; it does not mean that something positive is established.

If, however, one asserts the second type of destruction, which is the characteristic of arising as a dissimilar moment, then it is not established as being causeless. This is because it is accepted that such a moment arises specifically through the power of causes such as a hammer. For that very reason, it does not arise at the beginning, because its own causes, such as the hammer, are not present at that time.

In order to establish the presentation of contradictions, the text says **the two types of momentary things** and so forth. Certain things act as causes for a gradual reduction, where moments are produced that are slightly diminished, greatly diminished, or extremely diminished. An example is the effect of fire upon cold and so forth. Others are not like that and are not the cause of decrease; for example, fire is the cause for things like smoke.

Among those causes of reduction mentioned first, although they exist in a relationship of cause and effect, the world, whose vision of knowledge is obscured by the <term>rab rib</term> <gloss>blurriness/cataract</gloss> of ignorance, falsely imagines them to be an actual contradiction. The phrase **manifold types** refers to the distinctions such as fire which contradicts cold, wind which contradicts a lamp, and darkness which contradicts light. In the ultimate sense, there is no such thing as an entity that is a harmer or an entity that is harmed among things. In things such as paintings, it would follow that there is no cognition of diversity. It is not the case that things like paintings possess a single nature of a "composite whole" <note>original: "yan lag can", referring to the concept of an "avayavin" or a whole that is distinct from its parts</note>. If one asks what they are, then, it is not correct to understand them as having various "conjunctions" <note>original: "ldan pa", referring to "samyoga" or the relation of contact</note> of blue and other colors, where the cognition is produced by that conjunction.

In this way, there are no various conjunctions. Why is this? Because they lack form <note>original: "gzugs med phyir", referring to "rupa" or visible matter</note>. Conjunction, which is an essence of a quality <note>original: "yon tan", referring to "guna"</note>, does not possess another quality called form. This is because qualities themselves do not possess qualities.

Suppose one argues that although the object of sound does not have a nature of various conjunctions, it is described by applying the metaphor of diversity <note>original: "sna tshogs pa", meaning variegated or diverse</note> because it shares common characteristics with the diverse nature of a composite whole, such as a variegated butterfly. To this, we reply: a mere metaphor is not a basis. This applies to the term "conjunction." Conjunction is not an object of metaphorical application.

If one says it is called "diverse" because it resembles diversity in that way, then in the case of a butterfly, there is no variegated nature of a composite whole. Even in each individual part, there is not the slightest cause for the metaphorical application of diversity.

If one argues that in both cases, the distinctness of the essence itself is the cause for the metaphor, that is not so. This is because diversity does not exist in the form of a variegated butterfly, nor does a nature of diversity exist in paintings and such.

Furthermore, if it were argued that in paintings and such, the metaphor exists because of the "inherence" <note>original: "samavaya"</note> of many things into a single object of conjunction, that too is not logical. In that case, regarding the parts such as blue and so forth, if there is inherence and conjunction, those individual parts do not possess a conjunction of a diverse essence. Rather, there are the individual essences of blue and so forth, because each one is distinct.

Because there is no connection to a single object, the meaning of a mere metaphor is also not logical. One might argue: although that may be the case, as one gradually sees the parts like blue and so forth in a painting, a "synthetic cognition" <note>original: "bsre bar byེད་པའི་བློ་", a mind that mixes or synthesizes</note> arises which thinks, "this is a single diverse essence," thereby producing a cognition of diversity.

Observation <note>perceptibility</note> is established when something is observed, or when it is not experienced but is not obscured <note>meaning it is potentially observable</note>. The establishment of objects is applied in two ways through the division of substance <term>dravya</term> and quality <term>guṇa</term>. In that regard, what is called "substance" refers to the two aspects of the object and the cognition related to the object. It is the conditioned entity itself, such as a flask, which is produced from a collection of causes and conditions and is capable of being established without depending on others. The phenomena <note>attributes</note> and the subject <note>the possessor of attributes</note> that rely on that are the "phenomena and subject of substance."

Qualities are the distinctions that characterize those conditioned things, such as impermanence and so forth. Those things established as the basis for the phenomena and subject are the second category.

If one asks: "In which category are form, sound, and so forth included?" In this context, they are included under qualities, because they are distinctions that rely upon the flask and such. Furthermore, when they are applied as phenomena of substance, they are established as the nature of things <term>dharmatā</term> in terms of phenomena and subject. Those which are established by their own essence should be understood accordingly.

In this matter, other disputants <note>referring to non-Buddhist schools like Vaiśeṣika</note> assert that sound, smell, and so forth should be considered substances themselves because they exist in locations separate from the wind, sandalwood, and so forth. The introductory narrative regarding the expiation offense of eviction <note>original: "bskrod pa'i ltung byed," referring to the offense of throwing a monk out of a communal dwelling in anger</note> consists of two parts: the prohibitive ruling and the allowance. 

Regarding the narrative for the prohibitive ruling: The Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying in Shravasti at the Jeta Grove in the monastery of Anathapindada. At that time, the Venerable Udayin said to the newly ordained monks:

Venerable ones, come here, let us go on a journey through the countryside! There we shall defeat our opponents in debate, proclaim our own fame, and acquire gains. You will not be burdened with the bother of carrying begging bowls, robes, water-strainers, bowls, or belts, nor with the tasks of receiving oral transmissions, reading, chanting, yoga, or mental cultivation.

After Udayin had encouraged them in this way, he led them to settle. When they arrived at the outskirts of a mountain monastery, the <term>gandi</term> <gloss>a wooden percussion instrument used to signal monastic assemblies</gloss> of the community's lodgings was struck. Udayin's attendants went inside, and after receiving lodgings for Udayin and themselves, they sat down. However, Udayin remained outside, distracted by worldly talk, and did not come in until nightfall. Therefore, the attendants prepared Udayin's lodging separately, and after asking one another for permission, they went to sleep.

If one wishes to remove <note>an offense or obstacle</note>, it is said that one must "take up and separate" <note>original: "mnod pa dang 'bral bar ro"</note>. If there is a fault of concealing a remaining offense <term>shispa</term> <gloss>an offense requiring purification</gloss> from the preceptor or the resident teacher, the Sangha <gloss>monastic community</gloss> must quickly offer assistance and guidance regarding punishments and the like, so that the individual may quickly "take up" the remedy and "separate" from the fault. After thus showing the rite of residence, the following is stated to explain the duties of residence:

"Apart from questioning, these things should be done for him."

This means that the resident monk should not merely ask questions; he must also provide assistance and guidance regarding the bowl, robes, and other matters mentioned above. If one asks how long after full ordination <term>upasampada</term> <gloss>the ritual of becoming a fully ordained monk</gloss> one must remain in residence before performing duties without asking the resident teacher, the text says: one who has not reached ten years since full ordination must not live without a preceptor or a resident teacher.

If one asks whether all who have reached ten years are fit to perform these three types of actions, the answer is "not if they lack any of the following qualities" mentioned in the sets of five. Even if ten years have passed, if one does not possess any of the qualities from the sets of five mentioned below, it is not appropriate to perform the three actions mentioned above. What are those five qualities? They are the ability to perform or cause others to perform the following: nursing the sick, clearing away doubts, turning back sinful views, and causing someone to leave a state of dissatisfaction.

Whether one can perform these four named actions oneself, or whether one is able to delegate them to another, is sufficient. Among these, "nursing the sick" demonstrates having the patience for suffering and possessing compassion. "Clearing away doubts" demonstrates expertise in the Vinaya <gloss>the code of monastic discipline</gloss>. "Turning back those who have fallen into views" demonstrates expertise in the Abhidharma <gloss>higher knowledge or metaphysics</gloss>. "Leaving a state of dissatisfaction" demonstrates knowledge of another's intentions.

Regarding the phrase "able to cause others to perform," this does not mean that one is unable to do it oneself. Why is this? Because the supreme branch of these qualities is expertise in the Vinaya; if one is not expert in the Vinaya, one cannot clear away doubts. If one then asks why it says "to perform or cause to perform," it is because some are tamed by one person and some by another. It is not that one delegates to another because of one's own ignorance, but because if another person teaches, that individual may be better tamed.

Regarding the statement "spoken first by those," here it should be understood following the principle that the final part is applied to the third portion. 

If one asks whether the completion of most of the words constitutes the completion of the act itself, it is for this reason that the text says, "when there is no subsequent part." The phrase "no subsequent part" refers to a sentence that has no further addition; when the final word of such a sentence is mostly completed, it is considered completed. 

In a formal motion <term>jñāpti</term> <gloss>the initial proposal in a monastic ritual</gloss>, when it is mostly performed, it is considered performed. In a ritual with a motion and one follow-up action <term>jñāpti-dvitīya-karma</term>, the expression of the ritual act itself is the part without a subsequent addition. In a ritual with a motion and three follow-up actions <term>jñāpti-caturtha-karma</term>, the third expression of the ritual act is the part without a subsequent addition. This is the meaning.

In this context, the scriptural source from the Narratives <term>Nidāna</term> <gloss>the background stories of monastic law</gloss> states: "Venerable One, while defining a boundary <term>sīmā</term> <gloss>a consecrated area for monastic rites</gloss>, if a monk performing the ritual dies and passes away while the boundary is being established, should we say the boundary was established or not established? Upali, if the markers <term>nimitta</term> <gloss>the boundary signs</gloss> have been proclaimed, then because the ritual was mostly performed, it should be said that the boundary is established. In the opposite case, it should be said that it is not established. The same applies to the boundary for nuns." This principle applies universally, which is why it is summarized here.

Regarding the phrase "to the subsequent words of the repeated performance," this specifically indicates that it does not refer to the non-subsequent words. The statement "if the markers have not been proclaimed, it is not established" means that even if the ritual is mostly performed, if the markers of the four directions have not been proclaimed, the act of establishing the boundary is not completed. This is because the ritual depends on the definitive establishment of the boundary. That establishment is called the "ritual act," and thus it must be known. 

The phrase "By 'perfectly abiding,' it is different from 'nearly abiding'" means that "perfectly abiding" refers to the holy life <term>brahmacarya</term> <gloss>pure conduct</gloss>, which excludes the vow of "nearly abiding" <note>likely referring to temporary or preparatory vows</note>.
